title: Construction & Environment
overview: How a house is built and how its systems work, then the hazards and disclosure laws that affect a sale. The exam hits hardest on vocabulary (framing members, roofs, house styles), quick math (roof pitch, R-values, tons, amps) and the lead, radon, CERCLA and PCDS rules. The theme: spot warning signs, disclose what you know and refer testing to professionals.

mustKnow: **Footing** = wide concrete base below the frost line that spreads the load; **sill plate** = first wood member, bolted to the foundation.
**Platform framing** builds one story at a time and is today's standard.
**Balloon framing** runs studs from sill to roof and needs firestops; **post-and-beam** uses heavy, widely spaced timbers.
**Joists** are horizontal, studs vertical and **rafters** sloped.
**Girders** carry the joists, often resting on **lally columns**.
**Headers** span openings; the masonry version is a **lintel**.
Interior walls can be **bearing walls**. Never cut a **truss** member without an engineer's design; structural changes need an engineer or architect.
A 2×4 is a **nominal** size; it actually measures about 1½ × 3½ inches.
**Gable** = 2 slopes; **hip** = 4.
**Gambrel** = 2 pitches on 2 sides (Dutch Colonial); **mansard** = 2 pitches on 4 sides (Second Empire).
**Roof pitch** = inches of rise per 12 inches of run; on a symmetrical gable or hip roof the run is half the span.
**Cape Cod** = 1½ stories with dormers; **Colonial** = 2 symmetrical stories.
**Raised ranch** = entry between levels; **split-level** = 3+ staggered levels.
**R-value**: higher is better and layers add; compressed batts lose R. **U-factor**: lower is better (U = 1 ÷ R).
A **BTU** heats 1 pound of water 1°F; **1 ton** of cooling = 12,000 BTU/hr.
For the AFUE (furnace) and SEER (cooling) efficiency ratings, **higher is better**.
**Forced air** = furnace, blower, ducts; **hydronic** = boiler, circulator, baseboards.
**Steam** heat needs no circulator pump; a **heat pump** moves heat and reverses to cool.
**Supply** lines are pressurized; **drain-waste-vent** lines use gravity.
The **trap** seals out sewer gas; the **vent** keeps traps from siphoning.
The **T&P valve** (temperature and pressure relief) keeps a water heater from bursting.
**Amps = watts ÷ volts.** Breakers trip on overload; service amps are capacity, while usage is billed in kWh.
**GFCI** = shock protection near water; **AFCI** = arc (fire) protection in bedrooms and most other living areas.
NY **home inspectors** are licensed: report within **5 business days**, confidential to the client, no referral fees to agents, no engineering.
**New-home warranty**: 1 year workmanship, 2 years systems, 6 years material defects (GBL §777-a).
**Amanda's Law**: carbon monoxide (CO) alarms wherever there's a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage.
Sellers of a 1–2 family home, condo or co-op give a **smoke alarm affidavit** at closing; the buyer has 10 days to report dead alarms, and the seller pays.
**Lead disclosure** (pre-1978): pamphlet, known lead and reports, warning statement; buyers get **10 days**; no testing or removal required.
**RRP** is separate: certified contractors, lead-safe work and the Renovate Right pamphlet; window replacement is never minor repair.
**Radon**: test the lowest lived-in level; fix at **4 pCi/L** or more (sub-slab depressurization); NY requires no test or mitigation at sale, but the PCDS asks.
**Friable** asbestos crumbles to powder under hand pressure and releases fibers; leave intact material alone and never sample it yourself.
**Mold**: fix the moisture first; there are no federal limits.
NY mold jobs over **10 sq ft** need a DOL-licensed assessor and a different licensed remediator; owners working on their own home are exempt.
**UFFI** emits formaldehyde that declines with age; **PCBs** are in old transformers, capacitors and fluorescent ballasts.
**Oil spills**: strict liability under NY's Navigation Law and a **2-hour** report to DEC, registered tank or not.
The **Safe Drinking Water Act** covers public systems only, so well owners test their own water; a **perc test** measures how fast soil absorbs water.
Filling a wetland can require both a **Clean Water Act §404** permit (Army Corps) and a NYS DEC permit.
**CERCLA** liability is strict, joint and several, and retroactive; defenses require **all appropriate inquiries**; lenders that don't manage the site are exempt.
**Phase I** = records, site visit, interviews (no sampling); **Phase II** = sampling; Phase III = cleanup; Phase IV = monitoring.
**PCDS**: 1–4 family homes (not condos or co-ops), delivered before a binding contract, actual knowledge, not a warranty; the $500 credit is gone.
Licensees **disclose known material defects** and refer testing; concealing a defect on the seller's instruction is misrepresentation.

traps.trap: Joists are the sloped roof members.
traps.truth: Rafters slope from ridge to eaves; joists are horizontal floor and ceiling members.

traps.trap: Any interior wall can come out.
traps.truth: A wall where joists end or overlap is probably load-bearing. Removing it needs an engineered beam and usually a permit.
Use the run (half the span): 8 ÷ 16 × 12 = 6 in 12, not 3 in 12.

traps.trap: A bigger rating number is always better.
traps.truth: A lower U-factor is better. Higher is better only for R-value, AFUE and SEER.

traps.trap: The lead rule makes sellers test or remove lead.
traps.truth: No testing or abatement is required. The rule requires disclosure of known lead and reports, the pamphlet, the warning statement and the buyer's 10 days.

traps.trap: Tenants get the 10-day lead inspection too.
traps.truth: Only buyers do; landlords still give the pamphlet, disclosures and warning statement.

traps.trap: Sellers hand buyers the Renovate Right pamphlet.
traps.truth: Sellers and landlords give Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home; Renovate Right is the contractor's RRP pamphlet.

traps.trap: Radon under 4 pCi/L means no radon risk.
traps.truth: No level is known to be safe; EPA suggests considering mitigation between 2 and 4.

traps.trap: Old asbestos is harmless because it was banned, but it still has to come out before a sale.
traps.truth: No ban date clears a house, and no rule requires removal before a sale. Intact material is often best left alone.

traps.trap: An unregistered home oil tank creates no cleanup liability.
traps.truth: Registration and liability are separate. Liability is strict, and spills must be reported within 2 hours and cleaned up.

traps.trap: If I didn't pollute, I'm automatically safe under CERCLA.
traps.truth: Liability is strict, so not polluting isn't enough. Defenses require all appropriate inquiries; a buyer who knew may still be a bona fide prospective purchaser.

traps.trap: A Phase I includes sampling and lasts five years.
traps.truth: A Phase I has no sampling; that's Phase II. For AAI it must be within 1 year of purchase, with key parts within 180 days.

traps.trap: A 100-year floodplain floods once a century.
traps.truth: It has a 1% chance of flooding every year.

traps.trap: A seller can still give a $500 credit instead of the PCDS.
traps.truth: Covered sellers must deliver the PCDS before the buyer signs; the credit ended March 20, 2024.

sections.heading: Codes, permits, inspections and warranties
sections.intro: Plans lead to a permit, code inspections and a certificate of occupancy; buyers add their own inspections.
points: **Plans** (blueprints) show the design; **specifications** spell out materials and workmanship.
The **Uniform Fire Prevention and Building Code** applies statewide except in New York City, which has its own codes.
The **Energy Code** sets minimums for insulation and windows.
Inspectors check footings, framing and rough-in plumbing, electrical and HVAC before the walls close, then the final work.
Electrical work is checked against the **National Electrical Code**.
A **certificate of occupancy** follows a passed final inspection. A change of use needs a new one.
Neither a certificate of occupancy nor a permit guarantees there are no defects or private restrictions.
Site review covers NYS DOH well and septic rules, drainage and grading, landscaping, shading, walks, appurtenances (rights such as easements) and zoning.
**Home inspectors** are licensed by NYS DOS. They need 140 hours of training, including 40 supervised field hours, plus an exam.
The inspector's duty runs to the client. The license number goes on every report and ad, and the report must list the systems observed.
An inspector may not pay referral fees or kickbacks to the seller or either agent, or inspect a property in which he or a relative has an interest.
An inspector also may not charge to repair what he inspected before closing, or take a fee contingent on findings or a closing.
Inspectors can't practice engineering, so structural concerns go to an engineer.
The **new-home warranty** covers single-family homes and condo or co-op units in buildings of five stories or less. It starts at first title transfer or occupancy.
A builder can exclude the new-home warranty only by offering a qualifying written limited warranty (GBL §777-b).
**Home improvement contracts** over **$500** must be in writing and include a mechanic's lien notice. Advance payments go into escrow unless the contractor posts a bond or letter of credit.
Every 1–2 family home and condo or co-op unit needs a working smoke alarm. Battery-only alarms sold since April 1, 2019 must have sealed 10-year batteries.
**Amanda's Law** adds carbon monoxide (CO) alarms wherever there is a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage.

sections.heading: Foundations, drainage and moisture
sections.intro: The foundation carries the load to the soil, and most foundation problems start with water.
points: The **footing** is the wide concrete base under walls and columns. It spreads the load over more soil and sits below the frost line so frost can't heave it.
**Foundation walls** rest on the footings. They are poured concrete, block, or in older homes stone or brick.
Wall height decides basement versus crawl space. Full basements are the most common foundation in New York.
A **monolithic** slab is poured together with its footing; a **floating** slab is poured separately.

Keep water out: ground sloping away (about 6 inches of drop in the first 10 feet), working gutters, footing drains, a sump pump, dampproofed walls and vapor barriers under slabs and over crawl-space soil.
Red flags: **efflorescence** (a white mineral crust left by water moving through masonry), musty basements, and horizontal cracks or bowing in block walls.

sections.heading: Framing methods and structural members
sections.intro: Loads flow from rafters or trusses through joists, studs, bearing walls, girders and columns down to the footings.
points: **Platform framing** builds each story on its own deck, which acts as a firestop. It is the standard method.
**Balloon framing** runs studs from sill to rafters, so the open cavities spread fire unless **firestops** are added.
**Post-and-beam** uses heavy, widely spaced timbers, allowing open rooms and exposed beams.
Studs sit 16 or 24 inches **on center**.
Lumber goes by **nominal size**: a 2×4 is about 1½ × 3½ inches, a 2×6 about 1½ × 5½.
Cutting a bearing wall, girder or truss needs a fix designed by an engineer or architect, and usually a permit.
Some texts call the double top plate a flitch beam. A true **flitch beam** is a steel plate bolted between wood members.

sections.heading: Roofs, exterior and interior finish
sections.intro: Roof questions come down to counting slopes and sides.
points: **Ridge** = the peak; **eaves** = the lower edges that overhang the walls.
**Soffit** = the underside of the overhang; **fascia** = the trim board on the roof edge.
**Flashing** = metal or membrane that seals joints at chimneys, valleys and walls.
Asphalt shingles are the most common roofing, and slate lasts longest. Flat roofs use membrane or built-up roofing.
Attic ventilation (soffit and ridge vents), together with insulation and air sealing, helps prevent **ice dams**.
The PCDS asks the roof type, its age and any transferable warranty.
Outside: sheathing, house wrap, then **siding** and roofing.
Inside: after rough-ins pass inspection come insulation and **drywall** (gypsum wallboard or plasterboard). Older homes have plaster on lath.
Older textbooks may state pitch as rise ÷ span (8 ÷ 32 = ¼ pitch). That is the same roof as 6 in 12. Answer pitch questions as rise per 12 inches of run.

example.title: Worked example: roof pitch
steps: A gable roof spans 32 feet and the ridge rises 8 feet above the walls.
Step 1: Run = 32 ÷ 2 = 16 feet.
Answer: 6 in 12. Using the full span gives the wrong 3 in 12.

sections.intro: Questions describe a house and ask for its style.
points: Symmetry signals Colonial, Federal or Greek Revival; asymmetry, towers and ornate trim signal Victorian.
Count stories: ranch 1, Cape Cod 1½, Colonial 2, split-level 3 or more staggered levels.
The roof can name the style: gambrel = Dutch Colonial, mansard = Second Empire, long rear slope = saltbox.

sections.heading: Insulation, windows and ventilation
sections.intro: The building envelope separates conditioned space from the outdoors.
points: **R-value** (R-factor) is resistance to heat flow. Higher is better, and layers add.
Typical R-values: R-13 to R-15 in 2×4 walls, R-19 to R-21 in 2×6 walls, and about R-38 to R-60 in attics.
Insulate wherever heated space meets unheated space: attics, exterior walls, floors over crawl spaces or garages, foundation walls and slab edges.
**Compressed**, gapped or wet insulation underperforms. Air sealing is a separate job.
In New York's cold climate a **vapor retarder**, where used, goes on the warm (interior) side.
The **U-factor** rates a window's heat flow; lower is better. Fog between panes means the seal failed.
**Double-hung** sashes slide vertically. Casements are side-hinged and crank out, awnings are top-hinged and swing out at the bottom, and hoppers tilt in.
Ventilation controls moisture: kitchen and bath exhaust, heat or energy recovery ventilators (HRVs or ERVs) in tight homes, and attic and crawl-space vents.
Fuel-burning equipment also needs combustion air and a flue.

head: Insulation
Typical use
About R per inch
rows: Walls, rim joists, roof lines; seals air

example.title: Worked example: adding attic insulation
steps: An R-11 attic gets 8 inches of cellulose rated R-3.5 per inch.
Step 1: New layer = 8 × 3.5 = R-28.
Step 2: Total = 11 + 28 = R-39.
Step 3: U = 1 ÷ R. Before: 1 ÷ 11 ≈ 0.091.
Step 5: Heat loss = U × area × temperature difference. For 1,000 sq ft and 40°F, that is about 3,640 BTU/hr before.
Step 6: After, it is about 1,030 BTU/hr.
Answer: R-39, cutting ceiling heat loss about 72%. Traps: R-28, R-14.5, R-88.

sections.heading: Heating, cooling and heat pumps
sections.intro: Separate the distribution system (air, water, steam) from the fuel (oil, gas, electricity).
points: One **BTU** raises 1 pound of water 1°F.
Capacity is rated in BTU per hour. Air conditioners are rated in **tons** (12,000 BTU/hr each).
Size equipment from a load calculation (area, insulation, windows, foundation, ventilation), not from room count.
**AFUE** (annual fuel utilization efficiency) is the share of fuel delivered as heat.
**SEER** (now SEER2) rates cooling, and HSPF rates heat-pump heating. For all three ratings, higher is better.
Condensing furnaces (90%+) vent through PVC pipe.
Fuels are gas or propane, oil (in an aboveground or underground tank) and electricity.
Electric resistance heat needs no flue but is costly to run in New York.
Central AC has an outdoor **compressor** and condenser and an indoor **evaporator coil**. Integral systems share the furnace's ducts.
Homes use air-cooled condensers; big buildings may use water-cooled ones.
**Heat pumps** move heat with refrigerant and reverse to cool. Air-to-air is most common; water-source and geothermal units also exist.
Modern cold-climate heat pumps heat well below 32°F; older ones relied on backup heat.
**Freon (R-22)** is no longer made. Refrigerant must be recovered, not vented (Clean Air Act).
Rough lifespans: furnace 15–20 years, boiler 15–30+, AC or heat pump 10–15, tank water heater 10–15.

rows: Furnace, blower, supply ducts, return registers, filter

example.title: Worked example: tons and AFUE
steps: Step 1: A cooling load of 42,000 BTU/hr ÷ 12,000 = 3.5 tons. Dividing by 10,000 gives the wrong 4.2.
Step 2: A furnace with 90,000 BTU/hr input at 80% AFUE delivers 90,000 × 0.80 = 72,000 BTU/hr.
Step 3: The other 18,000 BTU/hr is lost.
Step 4: Electric heat: 1 watt = 3.412 BTU/hr, so a 1,500-watt heater gives about 5,100 BTU/hr.
Answer: 3.5 tons and 72,000 BTU/hr. The trap 112,500 wrongly divides by 0.80.

sections.heading: Plumbing, wells and septic systems
sections.intro: Two separate systems: pressurized supply in, gravity drainage out.
points: **Supply** lines run under pressure, about 40–80 psi. Pressure above 80 calls for a pressure-reducing valve. Undersized or clogged pipes cut the flow.
**Drain-waste-vent** lines slope (typically ¼ inch per foot) so waste drains by gravity to the soil stack and on to the sewer or septic system.
Each fixture has a **trap** holding a water seal against sewer gas.
**Vents** through the roof admit air so traps aren't siphoned. A blocked vent causes gurgling and sewer odor.
Water heaters: gas, electric or oil tanks (often 40–60 gallons), tankless units, or indirect tanks and tankless coils run off the boiler.
The **T&P relief valve** (temperature and pressure) releases water if temperature or pressure gets too high.
The **thermocouple** shuts off the gas when the pilot goes out.
Bacteria are the top drinking-water threat. Hardness causes scale, not illness. Acidic (low-pH) water corrodes pipes and can leach lead.
Private **wells** are the owner's job; the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) covers public systems only.
EPA suggests yearly well tests at a NYS DOH-certified lab for coliform bacteria, nitrates, dissolved solids and pH.
NY has no statewide test-at-sale rule for wells, though some counties (Westchester, for one) require one.
**Septic** system: house sewer, then the **septic tank** (solids settle), distribution box, and absorption field or seepage pit.
The tank is sized by bedrooms and the field by the **perc test** (10 NYCRR Appendix 75-A). Conventional fields need **1–60 minutes per inch**.
A NY-licensed engineer or architect designs the system. The health department approves it and keeps the as-built drawings.
The septic tank needs periodic pumping.

example.title: Worked example: NY septic sizing
steps: Rule: 1–3 bedrooms need a 1,000-gallon tank; add 250 gallons per added bedroom.
Step 1: A garbage grinder counts as one more bedroom, so a 4-bedroom house with a disposal is sized as 5.
Step 3: Place the tank at least 50 feet and the absorption field at least 100 feet from the well.
Answer: 1,500 gallons.

sections.heading: Electrical systems
sections.intro: Voltage pushes, amperage flows and watts measure power.
points: Power comes overhead (**service drop**) or underground (**service lateral**). The owner is generally responsible for the service equipment and all wiring inside.
Homes get **120/240 volts** (older texts say 110/220): 120 for lights and outlets, 240 for ranges, dryers and central AC.
**Service size** is capacity: 100–200 amps today, and 60 is usually inadequate. Usage is billed in kWh.
The service-entrance cables, not the number of fuses or breakers, are the sure sign of service size.
The PCDS asks the amperage and whether the panel has breakers or fuses.
**Fuses** melt and must be replaced; **breakers** trip and reset. Branch circuits are usually 15 or 20 amps.
Copper is the standard conductor. **Aluminum branch wiring** (about 1965–1973) can overheat at connections.
Knob-and-tube wiring (pre-1940s) is ungrounded.
Refer wiring concerns to a licensed electrician; never open a panel.

head: Term
Meaning
Exam angle
rows: Ground-fault circuit interrupter; cuts power on a ground fault
Arc-fault circuit interrupter; detects arcing in damaged wiring

example.title: Worked example: amps and service capacity
steps: A 1,500 W heater and a 1,200 W microwave share a 120-volt, 20-amp circuit.
Step 1: Total load = 1,500 + 1,200 = 2,700 W.
Step 2: 2,700 ÷ 120 = 22.5 amps. That's over 20, so the breaker trips.
Step 3: Continuous loads should stay at or under 80% of the rating (16 amps on 20).
Step 4: Service capacity = volts × amps: 200 × 240 = 48,000 W.
Step 5: A 60-amp service gives 14,400 W.
Answer: 22.5 amps. Dividing by 240 (11.25) or 100 (27) are the traps.

sections.heading: Environmental hazards at a glance
sections.intro: Know each hazard's source, risk and response, then refer to qualified testers.
points: **Asbestos** can't be identified by sight. It causes asbestosis, lung cancer and **mesothelioma** decades after exposure.
Asbestos testing uses bulk, air and wipe sampling. The fixes are **encapsulation** (sealing), **enclosure** (covering) or removal.
NY's Department of Labor licenses asbestos contractors and generally requires a survey before demolition or renovation permits.
**Radon** is an odorless, invisible radioactive gas. It enters through cracks, sumps, drains and well water, and tight new homes can trap it.
Radon is the **leading cause of lung cancer in nonsmokers**. EPA estimates 1 in 15 homes run high.
Short-term radon tests take 2–90 days with the house closed.
Radon-resistant construction uses gravel, plastic sheeting, sealing and a vent pipe.
**Lead** comes from pre-1978 paint and dust, soil, lead service lines and lead solder (banned in 1986).
Lead causes lasting brain and nerve damage in **children under 6**. Adults risk high blood pressure and kidney damage.
**Sick building syndrome** means symptoms tied to time in a building with no identifiable cause; a building-related illness has one.
**Wood-destroying insects**: termites build mud tubes and eat wood. Carpenter ants nest in wood and leave coarse frass but don't eat it.
Powderpost beetles leave tiny holes and fine powder; carpenter bees bore ½-inch holes.
**EMFs** (electromagnetic fields) have no federal standard and no proven harm.
NY's Public Service Commission caps new transmission lines at **200 milligauss** at the edge of the right-of-way.

sections.heading: Lead-based paint: disclosure vs. RRP
sections.intro: The disclosure rule governs information in sales and leases (Title X §1018, EPA and HUD, 1996). The Renovation, Repair and Painting (RRP) rule governs paid work that disturbs paint.
points: **Target housing** = built before 1978. Elderly or disabled housing and zero-bedroom units are exempt unless a child under 6 lives or is expected to live there.
Co-op sales and sales to investors are covered.
Before a buyer or tenant is bound, they must get the pamphlet, known lead information and reports, and the **Lead Warning Statement**, and sign acknowledgments.
Only buyers get **10 days** to inspect, which can be changed or waived in writing. Keep records **3 years**.
Agents must inform the seller and ensure compliance, and must refuse to hide a known lead report.
An agent who complied isn't liable for facts the seller hid. A buyer's agent paid only by the buyer isn't covered.
Exempt: foreclosure sales, leases of 100 days or less with no renewal, leases of certified lead-free units, and renewals after full disclosure.
Knowing violators face penalties and **triple damages**.

sections.heading: Environmental laws, tanks, wetlands and flood zones
sections.intro: Match each law to its job, then learn New York's tank and wetland rules.
points: **Tanks**: a fill or vent pipe, or oil lines through a wall, signals a tank even in a gas-heated house.
Get closure records and a professional evaluation (tank sweep, tightness test, soil test). Pulling the pipes to dodge questions is **concealment**.
The Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC) says a buried tank 10–15 years old probably isn't leaking, but the risk rises with age.
Most home oil tanks (under 1,100 gallons) aren't registered with DEC, though Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester have their own rules.
Liability under the **Navigation Law** is still strict, and spills go to DEC within **2 hours**.
The only exception: a known spill under 5 gallons that is contained, stays off land and water, and is cleaned up within 2 hours.
Retired tanks must be emptied, cleaned and purged. DEC prefers removal; closing in place means filling with sand or similar.
Homeowners policies often exclude pollution cleanup.
**Wetlands**: filling federal waters needs a Clean Water Act **§404 permit** from the Army Corps, with EPA oversight.
New York regulates tidal (ECL Art. 25) and freshwater (ECL Art. 24) wetlands, and towns may add rules.
NY freshwater wetlands of **12.4 acres** or more are regulated whether mapped or not. The threshold drops to 7.4 acres on Jan 1, 2028.
Wetlands DEC mapped before Jan 1, 2025 are also regulated, and protection extends to a **100-foot adjacent area**.
On April 8, 2026 the Albany County Supreme Court annulled DEC's 2025 wetland regulations (6 NYCRR Part 664) but upheld the 2022 law.
DEC now requires permits only for previously mapped wetlands and those of 12.4 acres or more.
Get a current jurisdictional determination. The Adirondack Park Agency handles the park.
**Flood**: the Special Flood Hazard Area (100-year floodplain) has a **1% annual chance** of flooding; the 500-year zone has 0.2%.
Federally backed lenders require flood insurance there, and homeowners policies exclude flood.

sections.heading: CERCLA (Superfund) and site assessments
sections.intro: CERCLA can make an owner pay for pollution it never caused, so commercial buyers and lenders do due diligence first.
points: CERCLA (1980) created the **Superfund**. NY's Love Canal disaster helped prompt it.
**Potentially responsible parties** pay: current owners and operators, owners at the time of disposal, and arrangers and transporters who chose the site.
Liability is **strict** (no fault needed) and retroactive.
Liability is also **joint and several**: one party can owe the whole bill.
**Innocent landowner defense** (Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act, SARA, 1986): all appropriate inquiries (AAI) before purchase, and no knowledge or reason to know.
Title insurance, as-is clauses and seller indemnities don't create the innocent landowner defense.
**Bona fide prospective purchaser** (2002): a buyer who knows of contamination is protected if it did AAI, isn't affiliated with a liable party, doesn't worsen it and meets continuing obligations.
**Secured creditors** that don't manage the site are exempt.
AAI is usually a **Phase I** (ASTM E1527-21) done within **1 year** before purchase.
The Phase I interviews, lien search, records review and site visit must fall within **180 days**.
A **brownfield** is property whose reuse is complicated by possible contamination, such as an old dry cleaner or gas station.
NY's Brownfield Cleanup Program offers tax credits.

sections.heading: Property condition disclosure and the licensee's role
sections.intro: The Property Condition Disclosure Statement (PCDS) is the seller's disclosure for houses (RPL Article 14).
points: The form has **56 questions** covering general, environmental, structural and mechanical items.
Environmental questions cover flood zones, flood insurance and claims, wetlands, landfill, fuel tanks, asbestos, lead plumbing, radon tests, spills and mold tests.
Structural questions cover rot, pests and the roof. Mechanical questions cover water, sewage and electric.
The seller answers from **actual knowledge**, may check unknown, fills it out personally and need not investigate.
An as-is sale is still allowed.
A seller's agent must disclose known facts that materially affect value or desirability.
Hiding a defect on the seller's instruction is **misrepresentation**, with fines up to **$2,000** (RPL §441-c). If the seller insists, withdraw.
Stigma facts, such as a death on the premises, aren't physical defects and needn't be volunteered (RPL §443-a).
Spot red flags, state only what you know, and recommend inspectors and testers.
Never sample, diagnose or promise safety.

The PCDS exempts 14 transfers: court order, deed in lieu, deed of trust, foreclosure, power of sale, lender resale after foreclosure, fiduciary, co-owner to co-owner, spouse or lineal relative, divorce, government, never-inhabited new construction, sheriff and partition (RPL §463).
